claim: Complex animal behaviors arise from a flexible combination of stereotyped motor primitives.
source: Complex animal behaviors arise from a flexible combination of stereotyped motor primitives.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's context.

claim: The initiation of C. elegans escape responses is predictable, with the animal moving away from a potential threat.
source: The initiation of the escape responses is predictable: the animal moves away from a potential threat, a mechanical or thermal stimulus.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an observation about escape response behavior.

claim: The motor sequence and timing following escape response initiation are variable.
source: But the motor sequence and the timing that follow are variable.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an observation about behavioral variability.

claim: A feedforward excitation between neurons encoding distinct motor states underlies robust motor sequence generation.
source: We report that a feedforward excitation between neurons encoding distinct motor states underlies robust motor sequence generation, while mutual inhibition between these neurons controls the flexibility of timing in a motor sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutual inhibition between neurons encoding distinct motor states controls the flexibility of timing in a motor sequence.
source: We report that a feedforward excitation between neurons encoding distinct motor states underlies robust motor sequence generation, while mutual inhibition between these neurons controls the flexibility of timing in a motor sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Electrical synapses contribute to feedforward coupling between motor state neurons.
source: Electrical synapses contribute to feedforward coupling whereas glutamatergic synapses contribute to inhibition.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a finding about synaptic mechanisms.

claim: Glutamatergic synapses contribute to inhibition between motor state neurons.
source: Electrical synapses contribute to feedforward coupling whereas glutamatergic synapses contribute to inhibition.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a finding about synaptic mechanisms.

claim: C. elegans generates robust and flexible motor sequences by combining excitatory coupling and winner-take-all operation via mutual inhibition between motor modules.
source: We conclude that C. elegans generates robust and flexible motor sequences by combining an excitatory coupling and a winner-take-all operation via mutual inhibition between motor modules.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: The motor repertoire comprises a finite number of motor primitives that are stereotyped across individuals.
source: The motor repertoire, constrained by the biomechanics of gait, comprises a finite number of motor primitives that are stereotyped across individuals (Ahamed et al., 2019; Berman et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2018; Stephens et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Behavioral flexibility allows an animal to explore the action space and select better strategies for acquiring rewards or avoiding danger.
source: On the other hand, behavioral flexibility allows an animal to explore the action space, and to select better strategies for acquiring rewards or avoiding danger in a changing environment (Sutton and Barto, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Many factors contribute to behavioral flexibility.
source: Many factors contribute to behavioral flexibility (Dhawale et al., 2017; Gordus et al., 2015; Remington et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synapses are unreliable.
source: Actions may be generated by an inherently noisy system: synapses are unreliable (Allen and Stevens, 1994), neurons generate variable spike trains (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995), and neural circuits may operate near the edge of chaos (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neurons generate variable spike trains.
source: Actions may be generated by an inherently noisy system: synapses are unreliable (Allen and Stevens, 1994), neurons generate variable spike trains (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995), and neural circuits may operate near the edge of chaos (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neural circuits may operate near the edge of chaos.
source: Actions may be generated by an inherently noisy system: synapses are unreliable (Allen and Stevens, 1994), neurons generate variable spike trains (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1995), and neural circuits may operate near the edge of chaos (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neural networks have structures that shape population neural dynamics onto a low dimensional manifold where nonrandom and ordered activity patterns emerge.
source: On the other hand, neural networks, whether adaptive or hard-wired, have structures that shape population neural dynamics onto a low dimensional manifold, where nonrandom and ordered activity patterns emerge (Ganguli et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon a gentle touch to its anterior body, C. elegans ventral cord-projecting premotor interneurons AVA/AVD/AVE relay mechanosensory inputs to motor neurons and reliably drive a backward movement.
source: Upon a gentle touch to its anterior body, the ventral cord-projecting premotor interneurons AVA/AVD/AVE relay mechanosensory inputs to motor neurons and reliably drive a backward movement (Chalfie et al., 1985; Pirri et al., 2009; Wicks et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After reversal, C. elegans may or may not reorient its body via a deep omega turn before moving forward.
source: After the reversal, the animal may or may not reorient its body via a deep omega (Ω) turn, before moving forward (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Which action to select and when to execute exhibit trial to trial variability in C. elegans escape responses.
source: Notably, which action to select and when to execute exhibit trial to trial variability, and they can be coupled.
evidence: Stated as an observation about behavioral variability.

claim: A longer reversal is likely to be followed by an omega turn in C. elegans.
source: For example, a previous study (Gray et al., 2005) has shown that a longer reversal is likely to be followed by an omega turn.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mechanosensory neurons ALM/AVM can induce four different behavioral outputs: reversal followed by an omega turn, reversal followed by forward movement, pause state, or forward movement (no response).
source: Optogenetic stimulation of mechanosensory neurons ALM/AVM (Pmec-4::ChR2) was carried out with blue light (473 nm, 4.63 mW/mm2) for 1.5 s during animal forward movement. Identical stimuli could induce four different behavioral outputs: reversal followed by an omega turn, reversal followed by forward movement, pause state or forward movement (no response).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1A caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: The reversal length distribution during ALM/AVM triggered escape responses is broad and likely bimodal.
source: The reversal length distribution is broad (Figure 1C left) and likely bimodal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The type-I (RF) transition rate r1 rapidly plateaued in about one second during ALM/AVM triggered escape responses.
source: r1(t) rapidly plateaued in about one second, while r2(t) increased and gradually became the dominant mode (Figure 1C right).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The type-II (RT) transition rate r2 increased and gradually became the dominant mode during ALM/AVM triggered escape responses.
source: r1(t) rapidly plateaued in about one second, while r2(t) increased and gradually became the dominant mode (Figure 1C right).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Escape responses induced by a focused infrared laser light exhibited qualitatively similar statistics to ALM/AVM-triggered responses.
source: The escape responses induced by a focused infrared laser light (Mohammadi et al., 2013) exhibited qualitatively similar statistics to ALM/AVM-triggered responses (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 1D and citation to prior work.

claim: Population interneuron activities encode distinct motor states in C. elegans.
source: Whole brain and multi-neuron calcium imaging of fixed and behaving animals suggested that population interneuron activities, which perform sensorimotor transformation, encode distinct motor states (Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; Kawano et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and figures showing calcium imaging data.

claim: Several interneurons including AVA, AVE, AIB, and RIM exhibited increased calcium activity during a backward movement.
source: Several interneurons, including the ventral-cord-projecting premotor interneurons AVA and AVE, and the local interneurons AIB and RIM, exhibited increased calcium activity during a backward movement (Kato et al., 2015; Laurent et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2014; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations and figures showing calcium imaging data.

claim: AIB establish recurrent connections with the premotor interneurons AVA and AVE that potentiate backward movement.
source: First, AIB establish recurrent connections with the premotor interneurons AVA and AVE that potentiate backward movement either directly through chemical synapses or indirectly through electrical and chemical connections with RIM (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A showing circuit diagram.

claim: AIB form gap junctions with the inter/motor neurons RIV.
source: Second, AIB form gap junctions with the inter/motor neurons RIV (White et al., 1986), which play a role in generating a ventral-biased turning behavior (Figure 2A; Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RIV play a role in generating a ventral-biased turning behavior.
source: Second, AIB form gap junctions with the inter/motor neurons RIV (White et al., 1986), which play a role in generating a ventral-biased turning behavior (Figure 2A; Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: AIB exhibit ramping calcium activity during reversals.
source: Third, AIB exhibit ramping calcium activity during reversals (Kato et al., 2015; Laurent et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2014), and finally, laser ablation of AIB significantly reduces the frequency of reversals during food search behavior (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Laser ablation of AIB significantly reduces the frequency of reversals during food search behavior.
source: Third, AIB exhibit ramping calcium activity during reversals (Kato et al., 2015; Laurent et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2014), and finally, laser ablation of AIB significantly reduces the frequency of reversals during food search behavior (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ramping rate of AIB calcium activity during the type-II (RT) transition was significantly higher than that during the type-I (RF) transition.
source: Among trials longer than 1.5 seconds, they all showed positive ζ, which during the type-II transition was significantly higher than that during the type-I transition (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures with statistical analysis.

claim: Optogenetic activation of AIB alone reliably triggered reversals followed by omega turns.
source: Optogenetic activation of AIB (Pnpr-9::ChR2 or Pnpr-9::Chrimson) alone reliably triggered reversals followed by omega turns (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Figure 2—video 1), whereas strong optogenetic inhibition of AIB (Pmec-4::ChR2; Pnpr-9::Arch; lite-1) during ALM/AVM induced escape responses almost completely abolished omega turns (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Strong optogenetic inhibition of AIB during ALM/AVM induced escape responses almost completely abolished omega turns.
source: Optogenetic activation of AIB (Pnpr-9::ChR2 or Pnpr-9::Chrimson) alone reliably triggered reversals followed by omega turns (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Figure 2—video 1), whereas strong optogenetic inhibition of AIB (Pmec-4::ChR2; Pnpr-9::Arch; lite-1) during ALM/AVM induced escape responses almost completely abolished omega turns (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Persistent hyperpolarization of AIB by expression of exogenous potassium channels increased the no-response fraction to ~20% upon stimulating ALM/AVM.
source: We also generated transgenic animals in which AIB were persistently hyperpolarized by an expression of exogenous potassium channels (Pnpr-9::TWK-18(gf)). Interestingly, the no-response fraction increased to ~20% (70/332, p<0.0001, χ2 test) upon stimulating ALM/AVM in these animals and a significantly larger portion of responses were pauses (35/332, p<0.0001, χ2 test, Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Optogenetic ablation of AIB alone significantly suppressed the type-II transition rate.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic ablation of AIB alone (Pnpr-9::PH-miniSOG, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H; Qi et al., 2012; Xu and Chisholm, 2016) significantly suppressed the type-II transition rate (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<1e-20, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical analysis and shown in figures.

claim: RIM promoted reversals but were less important in modulating the type-II transition than AIB.
source: RIM (Figure 2A) also promoted reversals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and E–G), but were less important in modulating the type-II transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: AIB play an important role in promoting reversal and turning behaviors.
source: Together, our data strongly suggest that AIB play an important role in promoting reversal and turning behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: AIB and RIV exhibited sequentially activated patterns in immobilized animals.
source: Whole brain imaging in immobilized animals implicated that AIB and their electrically-coupled partners RIV (Figure 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) exhibited sequentially activated patterns (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work and figures.

claim: During the type-II (RT) transition, RIV calcium signal rose rapidly immediately before a turn began.
source: During the type-II (RT) transition, RIV calcium signal rose rapidly immediately before a turn began, whereas it remained largely quiescent during the type-I (RF) transition (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: RIV calcium signal remained largely quiescent during the type-I (RF) transition.
source: During the type-II (RT) transition, RIV calcium signal rose rapidly immediately before a turn began, whereas it remained largely quiescent during the type-I (RF) transition (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Upon stimulating AIB, RIV calcium signal rapidly rose in immobilized wild-type animals.
source: In immobilized wild-type animals, upon stimulating AIB at t = 0, RIV calcium signal rapidly rose (Figure 3C dark blue and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: RIV remained quiescent upon AIB stimulation in inx-1unc-9unc-7 triple innexin mutants.
source: To determine whether electrical synapses contribute to the observed functional coupling between AIB and RIV, we examined the effect of AIB stimulation in inx-1unc-9unc-7 triple innexin mutants. RIV remained quiescent upon AIB stimulation (Figure 3C red and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), indicating that gap junction coupling underlies AIB stimulation-mediated RIV calcium activity.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Gap junction coupling underlies AIB stimulation-mediated RIV calcium activity.
source: To determine whether electrical synapses contribute to the observed functional coupling between AIB and RIV, we examined the effect of AIB stimulation in inx-1unc-9unc-7 triple innexin mutants. RIV remained quiescent upon AIB stimulation (Figure 3C red and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), indicating that gap junction coupling underlies AIB stimulation-mediated RIV calcium activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant experiment data.

claim: Optogenetic activation of AIB was capable, but with less likelihood, to trigger a turn in inx-1 mutants.
source: inx-1 single mutants exhibit superficially normal forward and backward movements, allowing us to examine the behavioral requirement of INX-1. The presence of multiple innexins in many C. elegans neurons implicates that they may function redundantly at electrical synapses. Consistent with this notion, we find that optogenetic activation of AIB was capable, but with less likelihood, to trigger a turn in inx-1 mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Rescuing inx-1 in AIB was sufficient to restore the turning probability in inx-1 mutants.
source: Rescuing inx-1 in AIB was sufficient to restore the turning probability (Figure 3D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Multiple innexins between AIB and RIV, or parallel circuit pathways, enable omega turns in inx-1 mutants.
source: Because inx-1 mutants were still capable of generating omega turns, we propose that either multiple innexins between AIB and RIV, or parallel circuit pathways are at play.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observation that inx-1 mutants can still generate turns.

claim: A transient quiescence or decrease of RIV calcium activity appeared after optogenetic stimulation onset in moving animals.
source: When neural activity in behaving animals was aligned to the onset of optogenetic stimulation, a transient quiescence or decrease of RIV calcium activity indeed appeared after t = 0 (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: A convergence of excitatory- and inhibitory- inputs onto the turning module may result in delayed depolarization of RIV in a moving animal.
source: Delayed depolarization of RIV in a moving animal may result from a convergence of excitatory- and inhibitory- inputs onto the turning module (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed delay in RIV activation.

claim: The feedforward excitation between the backward module and the turning module takes the form of electrical synapses, likely between AIB and RIV.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that the feedforward excitation between the backward module and the turning module takes the form of electrical synapses, likely between AIB and RIV.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: AIB triggered ventral-biased turning behaviors did not require glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
source: First, AIB triggered ventral-biased turning behaviors did not require glutamatergic synaptic transmission (Figure 4A), thus excluding polysynaptic pathways via chemical synapses from AIB.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of AIB while inhibiting RIM did not modify the turning probability.
source: Our optogenetic activation of AIB while inhibiting RIM did not modify the turning probability, whereas activating RIM while inhibiting AIB significantly reduced the turning probability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Activating RIM while inhibiting AIB significantly reduced the turning probability.
source: Our optogenetic activation of AIB while inhibiting RIM did not modify the turning probability, whereas activating RIM while inhibiting AIB significantly reduced the turning probability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In eat-4 mutant, optogenetic activation of AIB robustly induced an omega turn that was preceded by a much shorter reversal.
source: In the glutamate vesicular transport deficient mutant eat-4, optogenetic activation of AIB robustly induced an omega turn that was preceded by a much shorter reversal (Figure 4A left and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Restoring eat-4 expression specifically in AIB significantly prolonged the reversal length before the onset of an omega turn.
source: Restoring eat-4 expression specifically in AIB significantly prolonged the reversal length before the onset of an omega turn (Figure 4A left, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Stimulating AIB while blocking chemical synaptic transmission from AIB triggered an omega turn preceded by a shorter reversal.
source: Likewise, stimulating AIB while blocking chemical synaptic transmission from AIB (Pnpr-9::TeTx) triggered an omega turn preceded by a shorter reversal (Figure 4A left and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The type-II transition rate r2 rose more rapidly when glutamatergic inputs from AIB were disrupted.
source: Consistently, r2 rose more rapidly when glutamatergic inputs from AIB were disrupted (Figure 4A right).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The triple GluCl mutant avr-14(ad1035);avr-15(vu227)glc-1(pk54) exhibited a behavioral phenotype resembling that of the eat-4 mutant upon optogenetic stimulation of AIB.
source: Upon optogenetic stimulation AIB, the triple GluCl mutant avr-14(ad1035);avr-15(vu227)glc-1(pk54) exhibited a behavioral phenotype resembling that of the eat-4 mutant (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: In some trials, AIB stimulation immediately triggered omega turns without delay in the triple GluCl mutant.
source: In some trials (19/112, p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test), AIB stimulation immediately triggered omega turns without delay (Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with statistical analysis.

claim: Postsynaptic GluCl receptors work synergistically in modulating the onset timing of a turn.
source: This suggests that postsynaptic GluCl receptors work synergistically in modulating the onset timing of a turn.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the triple mutant data.

claim: Pavr-14 and Pglc-1 reporters exhibited expression in AIY interneurons.
source: Using GFP reporter lines, we found avr-14, glc-1 and avr-15 expressed in many neurons. By focusing on overlaps with neurons known to encode motor states (Figure 2A), we found that Pavr-14 and Pglc-1 reporters exhibited expression in AIY interneurons, while the Pavr-15 reporter exhibited expression in RIB interneurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Pavr-15 reporter exhibited expression in RIB interneurons.
source: Using GFP reporter lines, we found avr-14, glc-1 and avr-15 expressed in many neurons. By focusing on overlaps with neurons known to encode motor states (Figure 2A), we found that Pavr-14 and Pglc-1 reporters exhibited expression in AIY interneurons, while the Pavr-15 reporter exhibited expression in RIB interneurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RIB calcium activity significantly reduced upon optogenetic activation of AIB in immobilized animals.
source: Consistent with a glutamate mediated feedforward inhibition, RIB calcium activity (Psto-3::GCaMP6) significantly reduced upon optogenetic activation of AIB in immobilized animals, which was not observed in the glutamate vesicular transport deficient mutant eat-4 animals (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The reduction of RIB calcium activity upon AIB stimulation was not observed in eat-4 mutant animals.
source: Consistent with a glutamate mediated feedforward inhibition, RIB calcium activity (Psto-3::GCaMP6) significantly reduced upon optogenetic activation of AIB in immobilized animals, which was not observed in the glutamate vesicular transport deficient mutant eat-4 animals (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Restoring avr-15 expression in RIB promoted a longer reversal before the onset of an omega turn upon AIB activation.
source: Moreover, restoring either avr-15 expression in RIB or avr-14 (or glc-1) expression in AIY promoted a longer reversal before the onset of an omega turn (Figure 4B and Figure 3—video 1) upon AIB activation.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Restoring avr-14 or glc-1 expression in AIY promoted a longer reversal before the onset of an omega turn upon AIB activation.
source: Moreover, restoring either avr-15 expression in RIB or avr-14 (or glc-1) expression in AIY promoted a longer reversal before the onset of an omega turn (Figure 4B and Figure 3—video 1) upon AIB activation.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: A rapid rise of iGluSnFR signal on RIB's neurites was followed by a slow decay upon persistent optogenetic stimulation of AIB.
source: After the onset of stimulation, a rapid rise (Figure 4E inset plot,~10%ΔF/F0) of iGluSnFR signal on RIB's neurites (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A up) was followed by a slow decay.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The glutamate signal decay dynamics was not observed in eat-4 mutant animals.
source: Such dynamics was not observed in the glutamate vesicular transport deficient mutant eat-4 animals (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A bottom).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: RIB, together with AVB, have been previously reported to encode forward movement state.
source: Local interneurons RIB, together with the ventral cord-projecting premotor interneurons AVB, have been previously reported to encode forward movement state (Gray et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RIB form gap junctions with SMDV motor neurons that have been implicated in ventral biased omega turns.
source: Moreover, RIB form gap junctions with SMDV (Figure 2A), motor neurons that have also been implicated in ventral biased omega turns (Gray et al., 2005; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RIB calcium activity declined during reversals, and rose during the type-I (RF) and type-II (RT) transitions.
source: RIB calcium activity declined during reversals, and rose during the type-I (RF) and type-II (RT) transitions (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which is characteristic of neurons in both forward and turning modules (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Activating RIB during reversals triggered a transition to either an omega turn or forward movement.
source: Activating RIB (Psto-3::Chrimson) during reversals triggered a transition to either an omega turn or forward movement (Figure 5B left).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Strong optogenetic activation of RIB during forward movement reliably triggered omega turns.
source: Strong optogenetic activation (635 nm, 3.75 mW/mm2) of RIB during forward movement reliably triggered omega turns (Figure 5B right and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Inhibiting RIB during forward movement led to a pause state.
source: On the other hand, inhibiting RIB (Psto-3::Arch) during forward movement led to a pause state (Figure 5B right and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: When RIB interneurons were directly inhibited, the type-II (RT) transition rate r2 plateaued at a significantly reduced value.
source: When RIB interneurons were directly inhibited to mimic an inhibitory synaptic input, either optogenetically or by an expression of histamine-gated chloride channels (Pokala et al., 2014), the type-II (RT) transition rate r2 plateaued at a significantly reduced value (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Optogenetic ablation or blocking chemical synaptic transmission from RIB led to prolonged reversals during ALM/AVM-triggered escape responses.
source: Optogenetic ablation (Psto-3::miniSOG) or blocking chemical synaptic transmission (Psto-3::TeTx) from RIB also led to prolonged reversals during ALM/AVM-triggered escape responses (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: RIV activity was preceded by a longer quiescent state when trials were aligned to the stimulus onset in RIB ablated animals.
source: However, RIV activity was preceded by a longer quiescent state when trials were aligned to the stimulus onset (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: RIB modulate motor state transitions in part through indirect modulation of the timing of RIV activation.
source: Thus, RIB modulate motor state transitions in part through indirect modulation of the timing of RIV activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RIB ablation experiments.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of RIV/SAA/SMB or RIV alone during escape responses promoted significantly longer reversals.
source: However, optogenetic inhibition of RIV/SAA/SMB or RIV alone by spatially patterned illumination during escape responses promoted significantly longer reversals (Figure 6B and Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The type-II transition was abolished in RIV/SAA/SMB ablated animals since animals could no longer generate a complete omega turn.
source: The type-II transition was abolished since animals could no longer generate a complete omega turn (Figure 6C upper panel), while the ability of direct transition from a backward to a forward movement remained unaffected and the type-I (RF) transition rate r1 remained similar (Figure 6C upper panel) to wild-type animals.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The reversal duration became much longer and approached 30 s in some trials in RIV/SAA/SMB ablated animals.
source: Notably, the reversal duration became much longer and approached 30 s in some trials, which had not been observed in wild-type animals (Figures 1C and 6C upper panel and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: During normal type-II transitions, persistent neural activity in the upstream backward module could be abolished through inhibitory feedback from the downstream activity in the turning module.
source: These results indicate that during normal type-II transitions, persistent neural activity in the upstream backward module could be abolished through inhibitory feedback from the downstream activity in the turning module.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RIV/SAA/SMB ablation experiments.

claim: The type-I (RF) transition rate and the mirror transition rate (FR) from a forward movement to a spontaneous reversal in wild-type animals are consistent with the homogeneous Poisson process at long timescale.
source: Both the type-I (RF) transition rate (Figure 6C upper panel) and the mirror transition rate (FR) from a forward movement to a spontaneous reversal in wild-type animals (Figure 6C bottom panel) are consistent with the homogeneous Poisson process at long timescale, leading to exponential survival functions (Figure 6C insets) — fraction of backward or forward movements survived to t (Berg, 1993; Stephens et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the text with citations and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The feedforward inhibition and feedback inhibition between the backward module and the turning module implement a winner-take-all computation for action selection.
source: Together, our data suggest that the feedforward inhibition (Figure 4) and feedback inhibition (Figure 6) between the backward module and the turning module implement a winner-take-all computation for action selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: The motor module with the highest level of activity stays active by suppressing the activities of other modules.
source: The motor module with the highest level of activity stays active by suppressing the activities of other modules.
evidence: This is a description of the winner-take-all mechanism.

claim: The rapid increase of RIV activity coincides with the beginning of an omega turn.
source: The rapid increase of RIV activity coincides with the beginning of an omega turn (Figure 3A and E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in figures.

claim: The experimentally measured type-II transition rate is well fit by the model equation incorporating short-term synaptic depression.
source: The experimentally measured type-II transition rate is well fit by Equation 4.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Feedforward excitation between the backward module and the turning module can reliably trigger an omega turn followed by forward movement through strong and persistent activation of local interneurons AIB.
source: In C. elegans, feedforward excitation between the backward module and the turning module (Figure 7A) can reliably trigger an omega turn followed by forward movement through strong and persistent activation of local interneurons AIB (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The action in a motor sequence can be selected through feedforward excitation, triggered by either external sensory stimulus or fluctuations of internal circuit dynamics.
source: In other words, the action in a motor sequence can be selected through feedforward excitation, triggered by either external sensory stimulus or fluctuations of internal circuit dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The timing of an action can be tuned by augmenting the feedforward excitation with glutamatergic feedforward inhibition between AIB and RIB.
source: The timing of an action can be tuned by augmenting the feedforward excitation with glutamatergic feedforward inhibition between AIB and RIB (Figure 7A), and likely by modulating the strength of inhibitory inputs through short term synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings and model predictions.

claim: A tyraminergic feedforward inhibition from the RIM interneurons in the backward module to the SMD motor neurons in the turning module was shown to suppress head movement during reversals.
source: Previously, a tyraminergic feedforward inhibition (Alkema et al., 2005; Pirri et al., 2009) from the RIM interneurons in the backward module to the SMD motor neurons in the turning module was shown to suppress head movement during reversals.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Feedforward excitation and inhibition are combined with a nonlinear activation of turning neurons to produce flexible type-II (RT) transitions.
source: We propose that these functional motifs — feedforward excitation and inhibition — are combined with a nonlinear activation of turning neurons (Figure 7D) to produce flexible type-II (RT) transitions.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: When the backward motor state is suppressed via the hyperpolarization of interneurons AIB, an identical mechanosensory stimulus is less likely to elicit an escape response.
source: We show that when the backward motor state is suppressed via the hyperpolarization of interneurons AIB, an identical mechanosensory stimulus is less likely to elicit an escape response (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mechanosensory stimuli were unlikely to drive other motor programs when C. elegans was executing a turn.
source: A recent study also demonstrated that mechanosensory stimuli were unlikely to drive other motor programs when C. elegans was executing a turn (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The inhibition from the turning module to the backward module may account for the observation that mechanosensory stimuli are unlikely to drive other motor programs during a turn.
source: We propose that the inhibition from the turning module to the backward module (Figure 7D) may account for this observation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for an observation from prior work.

claim: Omega turn is a motor state encoded by transient activity in RIV.
source: We view omega turn, a motor state encoded by transient activity in RIV, as a special manifold connecting two attractors represented by persistent activity in the forward or backward module (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of dynamical systems.

claim: A combination of feedforward excitation and mutual inhibition between motor states suggests a new way to control nonlinear dynamics towards a different fixed point.
source: Our finding — a combination of feedforward excitation and mutual inhibition between motor states — suggests a new way to control nonlinear dynamics towards a different fixed point (Morrison et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Laser ablation of AIB and RIM in the backward module differentially affect the probability of spontaneous reversals.
source: For example, laser ablation of AIB and RIM in the backward module (Figure 2A) differentially affect the probability of spontaneous reversals (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RIM showed increased calcium activity during reversals and promoted reversal upon optogenetic activation.
source: While RIM showed increased calcium activity during reversals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and promoted reversal upon optogenetic activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G), they were less important in modulating the type-II transition than AIB did (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Noises in a neural circuit contribute to behavior variability.
source: Our biophysical model suggests that noises in a neural circuit (Equation 2) contribute to behavior variability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the biophysical model.

claim: Stochasticity in neural dynamics and behaviors may allow animals to efficiently explore the action space.
source: We speculate that stochasticity in neural dynamics and behaviors may allow animals to efficiently explore the action space (Dhawale et al., 2017; Duffy et al., 2019; Tumer and Brainard, 2007); learning, by which functional connectivity between motor modules is modified through synaptic plasticity, may optimize action selection and timing (Sutton and Barto, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Learning, by which functional connectivity between motor modules is modified through synaptic plasticity, may optimize action selection and timing.
source: We speculate that stochasticity in neural dynamics and behaviors may allow animals to efficiently explore the action space (Dhawale et al., 2017; Duffy et al., 2019; Tumer and Brainard, 2007); learning, by which functional connectivity between motor modules is modified through synaptic plasticity, may optimize action selection and timing (Sutton and Barto, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The functional connectivity between motor modules in C. elegans consists of feedforward excitation and mutual inhibition.
source: We found that in C. elegans, the functional connectivity between motor modules consists of feedforward excitation and mutual inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Conserved network motifs may be distributed among mammalian forebrain and midbrain circuits.
source: Conserved network motifs may be distributed among mammalian forebrain and midbrain circuits (Fadok et al., 2017; Klaus et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other animals could use similar algorithms to organize neuronal activities into sequential states to drive motor primitives, by which stereotyped and flexible behaviors emerge.
source: Other animals could use similar algorithms to organize neuronal activities into sequential states to drive motor primitives, by which stereotyped and flexible behaviors emerge.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.
